articles.title: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence.
That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

articles.title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union - The Guardian
articles.summary: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams | European Union  The GuardianBooking.com faces ‘in-depth’ Brussels probe  Travel Weekly - HomeBooking.com targeted in EU investigation into phishing scams, fraudulent listings  ReutersUK plan targets scam compounds, Booking.com faces EU fraud probe over listings, US sanctions law firm in shadow fleet crackdown  LinkedInBooking Holdings Inc Stock (BKNG) Moved Down by 3.29% on Oct...
articles.full_text:
EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams.
The European Commission, which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money.
A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”
EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website.
Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover.
The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.
Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.”
The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street.
EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com.
Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds.
EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused.
The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk.
Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links.
Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.”
Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

articles.title: Britain near bottom of NATO rearmament table - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: Britain near bottom of NATO rearmament table  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
Britain stands thirty-first out of thirty-two NATO countries on an internal alliance measure of how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, with only Iceland lower, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets the figure against the government’s Defence Investment Plan and the warning that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030.
Dhesi said: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report states: “However, the current reality could hardly be bleaker. According to an internal document apparently drawn up by NATO to measure how effectively members are meeting their rearmament promises, the UK is number 31 out of 32 Alliance countries. Only Iceland, a country with no military capability, is lower on the table.”
Ed Arnold, senior research fellow for European security at the Royal United Services Institute, told the committee: “[s]o that’s a pretty poor position to be in… [a]nd the only way that you can increase that really is through cash because it’s all about fleet availability, it’s all about readiness to be out of the door as soon as possible and as soon as needed.”
The Defence Investment Plan published in June splits funding into two parts, investing £298 billion in the four years to 2029-30 to reach 2.7 per cent of national income spent on defence, and a period running to 2035 by which all NATO allies including Britain have committed to spending 3.5 per cent of national income on defence.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and the assessment of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030.
The committee concludes that the near £300 billion investment over the next four years represents the bedrock on which any British contribution to deterring or defeating Russian hostility against NATO from 2030 rests, and that the Ministry of Defence needs to enhance the readiness of existing military assets as well as investing in new capabilities.
A separate conclusion states: “Government is already investing in the Hybrid Navy and Atlantic Bastion concepts to deter and, if necessary, defeat those threats in the High North. However, Royal Navy equipment readiness and platform numbers in particular are currently far worse than the government’s stated requirements. With 2030 identified as a key date by which to be ready to deter or defeat any Russian threat, dramatic progress is required before the end of the decade to improve the availability and capabilities of the UK’s Armed Forces for operations in the High North.”
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, that every platform goes through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and that equipment is held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.

articles.title: Piyush Goyal to visit Germany and the Netherlands to strengthen trade, investment and industrial cooperation - India Shipping News
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal to visit Germany and the Netherlands to strengthen trade, investment and industrial cooperation  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI : Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal will undertake an official visit to Germany (22–24 October 2026) and the Netherlands (24–27 October 2026) to deepen strategic economic partnerships, expand bilateral trade and advance industrial and technological collaboration.
During the Berlin leg of the visit, Shri Piyush Goyal will participate in the Berlin Global Dialogue, engaging with international policymakers and global business leaders to highlight India’s macroeconomic stability, manufacturing capabilities and pivotal role in building resilient global supply chains. On the sidelines of the summit, the Minister will hold high-level bilateral meetings with the German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) and the Economic and Financial Policy Advisor and G7/G20 Sherpa at the Federal Chancellery of Germany. The meetings will focus on strengthening bilateral trade and investment corridors, accelerating technological and industrial cooperation in advanced engineering, green mobility and clean technology, and exploring market access and investment avenues arising from the ongoing India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations.
Proceeding to the Netherlands, Shri Piyush Goyal will lead comprehensive government-to-government (G2G) engagements in The Hague, holding bilateral ministerial meetings with the Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate and the Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation to explore expanded trade channels and green transition initiatives. The visit will also encompass key discussions with the King’s Commissioner of North Holland and members of the Dutch Parliament’s committees on foreign trade and European affairs.
Shri Piyush Goyal will be accompanied by around 100 businesses and startups in Germany and the Netherlands. The Indian business delegation accompanying the Minister will have a parallel programme in Berlin, which includes sectoral roundtables with German CEOs and Indian business delegates. The roundtables will cover automotive, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure and energy; information technology, artificial intelligence and services; agri-food, consumer goods and textiles; and healthcare, pharmaceuticals and wellness. The delegation will also participate in an India–Germany Investment Roundtable with Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) on investing and establishing operations in Germany. It will also interact with German innovation and research institutions and think tanks on industrial transformation, deeptech, microelectronics, skills development, and India–Germany trade, investment and resilient supply chains.
The Indian business delegation will also visit the Port of Rotterdam on 25 October 2026 to see the port’s logistics and supply chain infrastructure. On 26 October 2026, Shri Piyush Goyal will address businesses from both countries, along with the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, at the India–Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague. The Business Forum will be followed by six parallel sectoral roundtables and B2B networking, covering agri-food and food processing; high technology and innovation; sustainability and renewable energy; logistics and supply chain connectivity; manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods; and services and allied sectors.

articles.summary: Russian strikes hit Kyiv after Witkoff meets Putin  Al JazeeraRussia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine  The GuardianMassive strikes hit Kyiv hours after Putin agrees to fresh peace talks  CNNRussia bombards Ukraine after Trump envoy hails ‘humanitarian’ Putin  The TimesRussia bombs Kyiv and Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow, despite talk of renewing negotiations  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Russia and Ukraine have traded a new barrage of attacks after a United States envoy met Russia’s president in St Petersburg to push for renewed talks on ending the war.
Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight into Thursday killed at least four people and injured dozens, including four children, Ukraine’s national emergency service said.
Metro infrastructure was also damaged at the Pivdenny Bridge, which spans the Dnipro River, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Ukraine’s emergency service said two people were killed in a Russian strike on a market in the town of Lozova in the Kharkiv region. Rescuers found a body in a house in Kramatorsk after a Russian strike on a residential home and one person was killed in an attack in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
In Russia, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said two people were wounded after Ukraine launched a barrage of 630 drones on the region, 163 of which were sent to the capital city. He said most of the drones were intercepted.
The governor of the nearby Tula region said Russian air defences destroyed 70 drones. Another man was wounded in the Lipetsk region, its governor said.
The exchange of attacks came after US special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at Constantine Palace in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
During Witkoff’s visit, Russia released jailed US teacher Stephen Hubbard as a goodwill gesture, prompting the US envoy to praise Putin as a “humanitarian”.
US President Donald Trump later said he believed the Russia-Ukraine war may be as close as it’s ever been to ending.
But the Kremlin was more guarded. While it said Moscow was “in principle” willing to restart US-mediated talks with Ukraine, it warned there was little “substance” in Ukrainian and European peace proposals.
In recent days, a frustrated Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for heavily sanctioned Russia to sell diesel and reduce fuel prices sent soaring by the US-Israel war on Iran.
Trump also delayed a new wave of Russia-related sanctions, a decision he defended on Wednesday as necessary to secure Hubbard’s release.
Witkoff told Putin Washington was “grateful” for the diesel deal, which sparked outrage in Kyiv and across Europe.
The war, Europe’s worst since World War II, has killed tens of thousands of people since Russia’s full-scale February 2022 invasion of its neighbour.
Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday said “appeasement” would not stop Russia’s war campaign.
“Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war,” he wrote in a post on X. “Only strength will.”

articles.title: EU cloud sovereignty rules could cost €115bn, study says - IT Brief UK
articles.summary: EU cloud sovereignty rules could cost €115bn, study says  IT Brief UK
articles.full_text:
A study commissioned by CCIA Europe says the European Commission's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act could impose €115 billion in costs over the next decade - six times the Commission's upper estimate of €18 billion.
Prepared by the European Centre for International Political Economy, the report examines the impact of proposed EU cloud sovereignty rules. It argues that the Commission's assessment understates the financial effects on public budgets, software redesign and private-sector users in sectors including banking, energy, healthcare and transport.
The analysis focuses on Article 31 of the proposed law, which would allow sovereignty restrictions to extend beyond public procurement to essential private-sector activities. The study says that would sharply increase the economic impact because spending by essential entities on cloud services is far greater than public-sector procurement alone.
In what it describes as a conservative scenario, applying the rules to a quarter of essential commercial workloads would add €80 billion in costs, which it says were omitted from the Commission's official calculations.
The researchers also put direct public budget exposure at €33.3 billion. They say software re-architecting and code rewriting would account for 69% of the proposal's real-world impact, as companies adapt applications built on global cloud and AI systems.
The burden would not be spread evenly across the bloc. According to the study, the average cost across the EU27 would amount to €548 per worker over 10 years, but smaller, more open economies that rely more heavily on international software architectures would face higher costs.
Under the moderate scenario, Luxembourg would face costs of €1,711 per worker, followed by Denmark at €905, Austria at €900, Finland at €864, Ireland at €856 and the Netherlands at €762, the report says.
Policy dispute
The findings add to a sharpening policy debate in Brussels over how far the EU should push digital sovereignty in cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence. Supporters of tougher rules argue that greater local control over sensitive digital systems would reduce dependence on non-EU providers. Critics warn that broad restrictions could raise costs and limit access to established global platforms.
CCIA Europe is calling for a narrower approach. It says any sovereignty restrictions should apply only to sensitive workloads where public-order risks can be demonstrated, and that origin-based and nationality-based conditions should be replaced with technical safeguards based on risk.
The group also says trusted international partners with bilateral EU procurement commitments should be exempt from Article 18 country screening. It argues that the proposed framework could fragment the Single Market by creating barriers to overseas cloud providers.
Industry warning
Mitchell Rutledge, Policy Manager at CCIA Europe, said the Commission's cost assumptions did not capture the proposal's full effect on public and private users.
"Member States cannot rely on the Commission's incomplete estimates when deciding CADA's strict sovereignty requirements for cloud and AI providers. Taxpayers and businesses will foot the bill, yet the official assessment missed 70% of CADA's true impact," Rutledge said.
He said the increase would come not only from infrastructure changes but also from rewriting software across connected business systems.
"Governments must recognise that CADA's massive spillover costs for essential private-sector entities are not hypothetical but inevitable. Businesses cannot simply switch servers; they must redesign software and rewrite code across entire supply chains," he said.
The study argues that compliance would involve much more than moving data from one provider to another. Applications developed around existing global cloud environments often rely on integrated tools, interfaces and AI services, meaning any change in provider eligibility could require extensive redevelopment.
The report says this is especially significant for European software vendors and digital small and medium-sized businesses, which would need to alter products designed to run on international cloud architectures. That could affect both cost structures and delivery timelines, particularly in countries that rely heavily on cross-border digital services.
Rutledge said broad sovereignty rules would damage innovation and hit the most digitised member states hardest.
"These sweeping restrictions risk draining European innovation and penalising highly digitised Member States. EU decision-makers must refocus CADA on objective, risk-based security rather than discriminatory rules that fragment the Single Market," he said.

articles.title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order | Rafael Behr - The Guardian
articles.summary: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order | Rafael Behr  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
An election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currently on course to win next year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.
Le Pen has been boosted in recent days by scenes of city centres ablaze and shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.
President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.
Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu accused “ultra-left” provocateurs of stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered that violence was the natural byproduct of a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.
At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservative France. His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.
In the past she has been locked out of the presidency by coalitions of moderate and left voters rallying, often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.
Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.
Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.
France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology. Donald Trump explained that “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vance agreed that “western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.
Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.
This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.
In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.
Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.
That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.
This is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.
Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. For Rupert Lowe, leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.
Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks to amplification on X by Elon Musk, the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farage into an arms race in fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.
Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.
That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.
To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: In China, ECB makes case for euro liquidity lines - AOL.com
articles.summary: In China, ECB makes case for euro liquidity lines  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank can strengthen the euro's global role and amplify the reach of its monetary policy by providing liquidity safety nets to foreign countries, ECB chief economist Philip Lane said on Wednesday.
Speaking at a closed-door event in Shanghai titled "Monetary System Beyond the Dollar", Lane said demand for the ECB's recently expanded euro liquidity facilities had been strong, with more than 30 central banks expressing interest.
"Liquidity lines bolster confidence in the currency and reduce the associated risks, supporting its wider usage," he told the event, part of the annual Bund summit, according to prepared remarks.
The comments come as policymakers globally question the the long-term dominance of the dollar in light of US President Donald Trump's unpredictable economic policy.
Advertisement
Lane argued that greater international use of the euro would enhance the ECB's ability to deliver on its inflation mandate by extending the global impact of euro area monetary policy.
He said the ECB's EUREP facility, which allows foreign central banks to obtain euros against collateral denominated in the single currency, could boost bond markets in the 21-country bloc, particularly through increased purchases by official reserve managers.
ECB President Christine Lagarde said recently that the bank was also reviewing its network of currency swap lines, which allow major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the People's Bank of China, to exchange their own currencies for euros.
Lane said such arrangements can encourage borrowing in euros but should be reserved for central banks in economies with close financial links to the euro area and a clear capacity to repay euro liabilities.
(Reporting by Francesco Canepa; Editing by Jonathan Spicer )

articles.title: EU inviting disaster by imposing carbon tax on steel, says Goyal - Daily Pioneer
articles.summary: EU inviting disaster by imposing carbon tax on steel, says Goyal  Daily Pioneer
articles.full_text:
Author: Rajesh Rai
The European Union (EU) is “inviting disaster” by imposing a carbon tax on its steel products, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said here on Thursday.
Participating in the Berlin Global Dialogue, he also said the EU is “shooting” themselves in their own feet by bringing in more and more regulations, restrictions on themselves, and closing their borders, something which actually helped them become a developed set of nations.
“You put a CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) on yourself. You put a 50 per cent import duty to bring steel into your country. You’re inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up,” he said.
He added that through these battery of regulations, the EU is trying to voice an artificial situation onto themselves, trying to create boundaries into Europe, trying to bring in “absolutely ridiculous” at times standards or levels of protection to safeguard certain sectors, steel being one of them, and only hurting their own economy.
“Now, imagine going forward, every infrastructure, whether it’s a port or an airport or your autobahns in Germany or your expressways, your utilities, your water pipelines, you name the infrastructure with costlier steel, costlier aluminium, costlier cement, with all the overlay of CBAM and deforestation rules,” he said. He added that the EU has 75-77 regulations.
“We’ve lost count. You keep adding to your regulations, add to the burden of your industry, make yourself uncompetitive. And of course, in some sense, it’ll also create non-tariff barriers for others to trade with you,” Goya said. He cautioned that the world is a reciprocal world now.
“And I don’t say that. Much bigger leaders are saying that. And in this reciprocal world, you bring in a regulation and stop some other country from working with you. They’ll bring in two regulations, which will hurt your businesses,” he said.
He added that at the end of the day, cost of living in Europe will go up, business competitiveness will go down and inflation will be high. “You will not be able to compete in global markets. Your auto industry is suffering that already. I think auto sales are down from Germany by 15 or 20 per cent in the last decade or so,” the minister said, adding, “How will you be competitive in the future? You will ultimately outprice your industry.”
He added that India is working on increasing competitiveness and is also working at a win-win partnership with everybody.
“We’ve got fair, equitable, and balanced agreements with every one of the partners with whom we are working. At least in the last four or five years, post-2014 particularly, we’re forging friendships, basis competitiveness. We are building complementary strengths,” he said. (PTI )
He added that India would trade with countries such as Singapore, where there is no CBAM and deforestation.
India has raised concerns on multiple occasions over these regulations. Under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Indian exports of steel, aluminium, and cement to the EU could face tariffs of 20-35 per cent.
Goyal added that India accounts for only 3-3.5 per cent of global carbon emissions despite supporting 17 per cent of the world’s population.
The European Union’s anti-deforestation regulation (EUDR) is a form of a non-tariff barrier. The regulation imposes strict regulatory requirements on sectors such as rubber producers and exporters targeting European markets, as it is a non-tariff barrier.
Goyal said that the EU’s contribution to carbon emissions is “humongous” and it is about 20 per cent.
He noted that those nations used low-cost energy earlier to push through growth. But at present, India’s contribution is low, and even the per capita damage to the ozone layer or carbon emission is probably 7-8 times lower than in Western nations.
The minister said that India has about 17 per cent of the world population and it has the fastest clean energy programme.
“We are greening our steel,” he said, criticising developed nations for failing to meet their climate finance and technology transfer promises to the developing and less developed countries.
He added that the CBAM does not recognise the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

articles.title: ECB Caught In The French Drama - TalkMarkets - Howl.link
articles.summary: ECB Caught In The French Drama - TalkMarkets  Howl.link
articles.full_text:
Back in September, the ECB surprised markets with a more hawkish message, at least between the lines. With headline inflation higher for longer and core inflation expected to increase in 2027, the stage seemed set for at least one more rate hike at the December meeting. Some even speculated about a back-to-back increase in October.
One month later, and after a severe fiscal and political crisis in France, the ECB is unlikely to repeat the hawkish tone at next week’s meeting. At face value, macro developments since the last meeting would still justify another rate hike. Headline inflation increased again in September and most leading indicators point to continued resilience in the eurozone economy. However, the surge in bond yields on the back of the French crisis is already imposing a new restrictive monetary policy stance. In fact, the surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had roughly the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp rate hike. For France, it's closer to a 50bp hike. Or in other words, the bond market has taken over the ECB’s job.
All of this means that the ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December. This is when new staff projections will be available and when there will also be more insights into whether higher energy prices will eventually bring knock-on effects on the rest of the economy or not. In fact, there are three main parameters that, in our view, will determine the ECB’s path going forward: i) the length and intensity of the war in the Middle East. The longer oil prices remain elevated, the higher the probability of more rate hikes; ii) the knock-on effects of higher energy prices. So far, there has hardly been any pass-through of higher energy prices in the rest of the economy. If this remains the case, the need for further rate hikes drops. If it doesn’t, the likelihood of new rate hikes goes up. iii) France. Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely (and less needed).
Because it's France
Even if France does not play a role in the ECB’s policy statement next week, it will be an important element at the press conference. Political and fiscal concerns in France, and the resulting widening in French spreads, have raised questions about whether the ECB could intervene through the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase securities issued by member states whose financing conditions have deteriorated for reasons not justified by country-specific fundamentals. However, before activating it, the Governing Council considers a cumulative set of criteria to determine whether the countries concerned are pursuing sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. In practice, this includes compliance with the EU fiscal framework, which would, at a minimum, require the proposed French budget to be fully adopted.
The ECB has nevertheless left itself some discretion, stating that the intervention criteria “will be dynamically adjusted to the unfolding risks and conditions to be addressed”. This brings back memories of the famous “because it’s France” by former European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker. Generally speaking, the ECB will be in a difficult position: intervening too quickly in support of France may be viewed unfavourably by other member states and interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules. That argues strongly against early intervention. Also, don’t forget that the leadership changes at the ECB over the next months (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could also affect how the ECB views TPI.
Given the challenges of justifying the activation of TPI at present, we expect the ECB to adopt a three-pronged approach to address the French crisis.
- The first line of defence is a more dovish approach to policy rates. As bond markets are currently taking over the ECB’s job of inserting a more restrictive monetary stance on the economy, there is less need for the ECB to hike rates aggressively, or to hike rates at all. In fact, the ECB has already started to prepare for this option, as ECB president Christine Lagarde recently noted that “while growth has been resilient, since our last meeting long-term interest rates have risen notably, which will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise".
- The second line of defence would be a covert return to bond purchases. The ECB could instead pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio 'flexibly', sending a positive signal to bond markets. This had already happened during the Covid period.
- Last but not least, should contagion in eurozone bond markets intensify, we expect the ECB to eventually trigger the TPI. As long as France remains non-compliant with the European fiscal rules, the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France.
All in all, next week’s ECB meeting looks set to be uneventful on action but clearly not on words.

articles.title: EU carbon tax is ‘inviting disaster’, says Piyush Goyal - Livemint
articles.summary: EU carbon tax is ‘inviting disaster’, says Piyush Goyal  Livemint
articles.full_text:
Berlin: India’s commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday said the European Union’s (EU) carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), a tax on carbon-intensive imported goods, is “inviting disaster”.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue 2026, Goyal said, “If you have put a CBAM on yourself, you put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up. Your people will be unhappy. Your industry will be out-priced.”
For its part, New Delhi has secured commitments from the EU, including a forward-looking most-favoured-nation assurance that any flexibilities granted to third countries under CBAM regulations will also be extended to India.
Speaking separately at the inauguration of the India Centre at German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), Goyal said the India-European Union (EU) free trade agreement (FTA) may become operational within four to five months. He added that the proposed FTA with the 27-member EU is expected to be signed at the end of the calendar year.
“It will move very rapidly towards signature. And I want to thank all the countries of the European Union. Because this is one agreement and I urge you to reflect on the past: whether you have seen an agreement move with this alacrity,” Goyal said, adding, “the sense of urgency, the mutual commitment to make this happen was truly remarkable”.
The development is significant as India and the EU account for a quarter of the world’s gross domestic product and a third of its trade. India and the EU wrapped up talks for an FTA in January 2026, capping negotiations that were first launched in 2007, paused in 2013, and again revived in 2022.
Under the FTA, formally known as the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement, over 99% of Indian exports by value and 97% of tariff lines will gain preferential entry into the EU, unlocking opportunities for the country’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and creating jobs for women, artisans, young people and professionals.
According to the European Commission, the FTA will eliminate or cut tariffs on more than 96% of the EU’s goods exports to India, saving European exporters around €4 billion a year in duties. The EU has committed to remove duties on about 70.4% of tariff lines immediately, covering almost 90.7% of India's export value, with another 20.3% of products subject to phased elimination, and the rest seeing liberalization via duty concessions or tariff quotas. Immediate duty-free access to the EU will apply to all textiles, apparel, leather, and footwear; 94.4% of marine products; and 96.6% of gems and jewellery, with chemicals and base metals split between immediate and phased cuts.
For its part, India has promised immediate duty-free access on about 49.6% of EU tariff lines covering 30.6% of trade value, with 39.5% of lines covering 63.1% of value under phased elimination over five, seven or 10 years. India's total offer covers around 92.1% of EU tariff lines and 97.5% of trade value.
The conclusion of the FTA was jointly announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the 16th India-EU Summit in New Delhi on 27 January 2026. India-EU merchandise trade stood at €118.4 billion in 2025, with the bloc importing goods worth €69.5 billion from India and exporting €48.9 billion to India. The total annual bilateral trade in both goods and services was worth €180 billion.
“To my mind Germany’s precision engineering, your Mittelstand (medium-sized companies), commitment to quality with our desire to upgrade Indian infrastructure, our digital capabilities, our youthful, skilled and talented people, I think we can together shape an outstanding future to this evolving global order,” said Goyal, who is on an official visit to Germany and the Netherlands to deepen strategic economic partnerships, expand bilateral trade, and advance industrial and technological collaboration.
Germany is India’s largest trading partner in the EU. Total bilateral trade reached $31 billion in FY26, up 4.83% from $29.57 billion in FY25, according to commerce ministry data.
“Our ambition should not stop at Made in India or Made in Germany. We should look at [goods] co-created by us. We should look at becoming collaborators, to become competitive for the world. And towards that end, to turn that ambition into reality, we must connect trade with investment, manufacturing with research, and our industries with our academic institutions, so that we can truly bring the FTA to factories,” Goyal added.
Experts said India and Germany share a special relationship. “Germany is the strongest economy in the EU. We have a special relationship with it. Trade and investment linkages are the strongest in the EU. For Germany India- EU FTA is of immense interest,” said Dammu Ravi, India’s former economic relations secretary in the ministry of external affairs. He added that Germany’s Mittelstand, or medium-sized businesses, offer vital opportunities for Indian MSMEs to partner and build global competitiveness.
The writer is in Berlin as the guest of Confederation of Indian Industry.

articles.title: From Kyiv with love (and savings): A defence win-win for Europe and Ukraine - CEPR
articles.summary: From Kyiv with love (and savings): A defence win-win for Europe and Ukraine  CEPR
articles.full_text:
A euro goes three to five times further in Ukraine
The rearmament debate often focuses on spending rather than what it buys. Robertson's military purchasing power parity index prices personnel, operations and equipment at local costs. On his estimates, a euro buys roughly three to five times more defence in Ukraine than in a high-wage economy such as Germany (Robertson 2021, 2025).
Unit costs tell the same story.
- Soldiers. Dividing defence budgets by active personnel gives a rough all-in cost per soldier. Germany's 2026 budget works out at about €580,000 per soldier, Ukraine's at €85,000–106,000, or €118,000–148,000 if partner aid outside the budget is included. Even Poland spends about twice as much per soldier as Ukraine (Figure 1). Pay, not quality, explains much of the gap: a new German volunteer earns at least €2,600 a month, a Ukrainian soldier in a rear area about €780. 
- Artillery. Ukraine's 155mm Bohdana self-propelled howitzer costs about €2.3–2.8 million (Kirkegaard 2025). For the price of one German PzH 2000, an army could field about seven Bohdanas; for one Swedish Archer, about four (Figure 2). The German gun is more sophisticated, but in a war of attrition the number of barrels in action matters at least as much.
- Drones and air defence. A Ukrainian first-person-view attack drone costs about $500 to produce; comparable drones ordered by a European coalition cost roughly four times as much. Ukrainian interceptor drones costing $1,000–2,500 bring down Russia’s Shaheds worth $20,000–50,000, whereas an IRIS-T missile costs $430,000–500,000 per shot and a Patriot about $4 million. The 2026 Iran war showed what happens when that equation runs the other way, as Gulf states fired hundreds of Patriots at cheap drones (Burilkov and Wolff 2026).
Figure 1 Defence spending per active soldier
    
  
      
  
Sources: NATO (2025a) estimates for 2025, converted at NATO exchange rates; Ukraine from its amended 2026 budget; see Gorodnichenko and Becker (2026) for more details.
Figure 2 The cost of self-propelled howitzers
    
  
      
  
Source: Mejino-López and Wolff (2024).
Timing is (sometimes) everything
Price matters, but timing may matter more: a howitzer delivered in two months deters in a way that a better one delivered in three years cannot. When Denmark began paying Ukrainian manufacturers directly in 2024, the first 18 Bohdanas were handed over within about two months. Output rose from about six guns a month in early 2023 to about 40 by late 2025. Germany ordered ten PzH 2000s in March 2023 to replace guns given to Ukraine. The first new gun rolled out in November 2025, with further lots scheduled for 2027–2029. France's CAESAR line, Europe's fastest-growing, aims for 12 a month in 2026, less than a third of the Bohdana's rate.
Drones show the same pattern. Ukraine produced about 2.2 million in 2024 and is on track for 5–6 million this year; officials say 20 million a year would be possible if allies paid for them (Horowitz et al. 2026). Ukraine's defence production capacity has grown roughly 35-fold since 2022, yet the Council on Foreign Relations estimates that $25–40 billions of it stands idle for lack of orders (Horowitz et al. 2026). Ukraine cannot close that gap itself. Tax revenues are already projected at about 39% of GDP, and the IMF projects a significant external financing gap of $52 billion for 2026 (IMF 2026).
Europe faces a time constraint on soldiers too. Despite its best recruiting year since conscription was suspended, the Bundeswehr grew by only about 4,000 soldiers net over the past year (BMVg 2026). At that pace, its target of 260,000 would take close to two decades to reach. Europe is short of time as well as money, whereas Ukrainian capacity can be activated within months.
‘Saving’ money today is expensive in the longer run
Every month of war kills soldiers and civilians and destroys homes, power plants and railways. Reconstruction needs are already estimated at nearly three times Ukraine's annual GDP (World Bank 2026), a bill the EU will largely share. A Russian victory would put an emboldened army along a far longer stretch of the EU's border and force permanently higher defence spending. With US support no longer assured, Europe, whose economy is more than ten times the size of Russia's, is the only power able to make the difference.
Insecurity also raises the price of money. If fear of war takes hold, Europeans could pay a risk premium on everything they borrow, much like the 'Korea discount' long applied to South Korean assets (Becker et al. 2025). EU governments owe about €15.7 trillion (Eurostat 2026). Once that debt is refinanced, each basis point added to borrowing costs would cost about €1.6 billion a year. 
Two objections deserve a brief answer. First, a euro spent at home partly returns as tax revenue, but even if 40 cents came back, a German soldier would still cost two to four times as much as a Ukrainian one. Second, Ukrainian prices will rise with demand, but with $25–40 billion of idle capacity that limit is still some way off.
Send the bill to Moscow
Russia's own money can ease Europe's fiscal constraint. About €210 billion of Russian central bank reserves are immobilised in the EU, mostly at Euroclear in Brussels. In December 2025, the EU set aside a plan to lend against these assets and agree to borrow €90 billion on capital markets instead. The ECB has warned of risks to the euro's international role, but EU bond yields have not reacted so far (Havrylchyk 2025). Denmark has already used proceeds from frozen Russian assets to finance Bohdana production. Using the assets themselves to buy Ukrainian weapons would make the aggressor fund the defence against it and expand Europe's fiscal space without new taxes or debt. For European taxpayers, it is the closest thing to a free lunch that security policy offers.
What Europe should do
Treating Ukraine's army and defence industry as part of Europe's own defence implies five changes, most of them about speed as much as money.
- Fund Ukraine's idle capacity predictably. Europe should commit a fixed share of its defence budgets each year to Ukrainian-made equipment for Ukraine's forces. Redirecting a tenth of the increase in EU defence spending since 2021 would roughly double the military aid Ukraine now receives.
- Sign multi-year contracts on the Danish model. Annual orders leave Ukrainian factories idle for up to three months between procurement cycles. Contracts of three to five years would let firms hire, invest and cut unit costs further.
- Count it as European defence. NATO's 2025 Hague declaration allows direct support for Ukraine's defence and defence industry to count towards spending targets (NATO 2025b). EU fiscal rules should do the same, and SAFE, the European Defence Industry Programme and the European Defence Fund should likewise treat buying Ukrainian as buying European.
- Build with Ukraine. Joint ventures with production lines on both sides of the border spread the risk from missile strikes, help replace Chinese components and keep know-how within Europe.
- Attach conditions that fit the purpose. Money for weapons should come with transparency, independent audit and anti-corruption safeguards on the contracts themselves. Holding it back until unrelated reforms are complete costs the one thing Europe is shortest of: time.
Ukraine: From cost to partner
Ukraine's army does not replace European armed forces but it strengthens them. Our argument concerns the margin: where the next euro buys the most security for Europe as a whole. Here Ukraine wins on both price and speed. Stronger support would also save lives, limit reconstruction costs and build an army and industry that can anchor Europe's security after the war (Gorodnichenko 2026). In 1941, the US Lend-Lease Act armed Britain and other allies as a strategic investment rather than charity, Europe should follow this example.

Reported by The Register. The European Commission has launched a formal investigation into Booking.com to determine if the platform is adequately addressing rising instances of fraud, phishing and smishing under the Digital Services Act.
The probe focuses on three primary areas involving the platform, which serves over 45 million users in the European Union. First, regulators are examining whether the company fails to prevent fraudulent property listings. Second, they are investigating if the site sufficiently counters social engineering and phishing attempts where scammers hijack owner accounts to solicit payments. Finally, the investigation assesses advertising transparency, specifically regarding how boosted listings are distinguished from organic search results. Officials initiated the inquiry following a significant surge in travel scams, with Booking.com reporting a 500% to 900% increase in incidents over 18 months. In the Netherlands alone, fraud reports increased tenfold in early 2026, resulting in 82,000 euros in damages. While the company maintains that it is cooperating with the European Commission and prioritizing user security, regulators argue that current risk assessment measures remain substandard. The commission expects more diligent oversight, including improved verification of property owners and faster removal of malicious listings to protect consumers and business users across all member states.

articles.title: What lessons can we learn to keep European industry competitive from the measures taken by Germany, as the cost of electricity continues to turn the screw? - Etudes Economiques – BNP Paribas
articles.summary: What lessons can we learn to keep European industry competitive from the measures taken by Germany, as the cost of electricity continues to turn the screw?  Etudes Economiques – BNP Paribas
articles.full_text:
The 2022 energy crisis clearly highlighted the issue of electricity prices in Europe — and, more broadly, the issue of energy prices. As a result, European manufacturers’ competitiveness has been severely undermined when compared with the United States and China. By reigniting tensions over electricity prices, the conflict that began in the Middle East in late February 2026 further underscores the continent’s vulnerability to fossil fuel imports, despite the expansion of renewable energy. Faced with an environment of potential sharp and sudden price rises, European governments do not have the same room for manoeuvre.
While the additional costs borne by European manufacturers are mainly linked to the share of gas in national electricity mixes, we will first illustrate that, in Germany, grid operation and maintenance costs, as well as taxation, are also contributing significantly to these costs. We will then explore the solutions proposed by the German government under the new European measures regulating state aid to electricity-intensive industries. Finally, our estimates will show that, while these measures make Germany more competitive against some European countries, they do not place it on an equal competitive footing with the United States or China. Nevertheless, Germany has made significant progress in decarbonising and making its electricity mix more flexible from a European perspective. This should help to ensure that electricity costs are reduced in the medium term.
Gas: a key factor in the additional electricity costs faced by European industry
European manufacturers are still paying significantly higher electricity costs than their American and Chinese competitors. In 2019, there was a 30% difference between the prices charged to European electricity-intensive industries (corresponding to the lower end of the industrial price range) and the average US industrial price. In 2025, it stood at nearly 100% according to the IEA (2026)[1], after peaking at an average of 148% between 2022 and 2023. There is currently a 50% difference with their Chinese competitors[2].
The disruption to Russian gas supplies since 2022 is behind the rising gas prices, particularly as the EU has had to turn to liquefied natural gas[3] (LNG), which is more expensive than gas transported via pipeline and, above all, exposes Europe to global gas market conditions. The growth of LNG has, in fact, intensified competition between the major consumption regions, primarily Europe and Asia. European and Asian prices now tend to move more in tandem (Chart 1). However, in China, the prevalence of coal — a widely available local resource — and a more regulated electricity price help to keep industrial prices lower. At the same time, the United States enjoys plentiful domestic gas, which is produced at a low cost, driven by the sharp rise in shale oil and gas production over the past decade. By contrast, since 2022, Europe has been more exposed to the cost of imported gas (90% of its total consumption, according to Eurostat), while the United States and China have enjoyed plentiful domestic resources.
The ‘merit order’ principle in setting electricity prices in Europe
Fluctuations and the level of gas prices are passed on to European electricity prices via the ‘merit order’ marginal pricing mechanism, with the wholesale price determined by the marginal cost of the last (and most expensive) electricity source called upon to meet demand.
As a result, gas plays a decisive role, with gas-fired power stations setting the price in around 40% of cases in Europe[4], with significant variations depending on national electricity mixes. It is close to this average in Germany, below it in Spain (26%) and France (17%), and above it in Italy (73%)[5] in 2025[6][7]. Therefore, electricity prices are still sensitive to fluctuations in gas prices, even when electricity is not generated from gas (Chart 2). This pass-through is particularly pronounced when demand rises and requires the use of more expensive sources, or when supply constraints arise (for example, during extreme heatwaves that reduce wind-power generation or disrupt the cooling of nuclear power plants).
However, for the time being, the 2026 energy crisis is having a far smaller effect on electricity prices than in 2022. On the one hand, the 2026 peak reached by the European TTF benchmark is still well below that recorded in 2022[8].
In addition, there has been significant progress in decarbonising European electricity mixes since 2022, which has helped to mitigate, on average, the pass-through of gas prices to electricity prices.
Some European countries have managed to stay competitive, but Germany is still the exception
Electricity prices partly vary due to countries’ electricity mixes (Chart 3). Electricity-intensive manufacturers in countries where the share of fossil energy is high face higher costs (Poland, Italy and Ireland) (Chart 4). Conversely, countries with a less carbon-intensive mix (particularly France and Spain in recent times) are less directly exposed to these fluctuations, with costs closer to the United States and China (Chart 5).
The situation in Germany is paradoxical, as, despite progressively greening its electricity mix and wholesale electricity prices (averaging 90 EUR/MWh over the 2023–2025 period) and average electricity costs (across all industrial sectors) in line with the European average, the most energy-intensive industries face higher costs than the European average (and even more so compared with international competitors). This is mainly due to grid costs and a tax burden above EU standards (Chart 6). In the first half of 2026, for the most electricity-intensive industries, the difference compared with the European average was 9%, based on the prices excluding taxes and levies provided by Eurostat. This gap is mainly due to the cost of accessing the grid. If all taxes and levies are included, the difference rises to 21% (Chart 7)[9].
Europe’s approach of adopting both structural programmes and targeted support measures
European programmes to support the low-carbon transition pursue objectives relating to climate action (reducing greenhouse gas emissions), sovereignty[10] (increasing energy self-sufficiency) and competitiveness (reducing the volatility and costs associated with fossil fuels). The RePowerEU programme, which was launched in 2022 in response to the energy crisis, primarily aims to reduce imports of Russian gas and, more generally, to accelerate the low-carbon transition. Although Europe has reduced its dependence on imports of Russian fossil fuels, there has still not been enough progress around the energy transition and cross-border connectivity. This is due to governance constraints and struggles in implementing the programme in practice within each Member State[11].
State aid is still the main vehicle for this. In response to the 2021–2022 energy crisis, the European Union temporarily relaxed the rules on this type of aid in order to support businesses facing rising energy prices. Any intervention of this kind, provided that it is selective and could affect trade within the single market, must be authorised in advance by the European Commission in principle. Since June 2025, the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF) has provided a more sustainable framework for these kinds of interventions. In particular, this framework, which runs until the end of 2030, authorises Member States to grant temporary aid to electricity-intensive businesses to offset the cost of electricity. The aid must be targeted and come with decarbonisation commitments[12]. Against the backdrop of the crisis in the Middle East, the temporary METSAF scheme, adopted in April 2026, helped (in relation to measures falling under the CISAF) to increase the proportion of additional costs offset by governments from 50% to 70%, thereby offering additional support to the most at-risk sectors.
Germany is still suffering from insufficient investment in its electricity networks, which the aid schemes are attempting to offset
The issue of electricity costs is a particularly hot issue in Germany, given the importance of industry to the economy (around 20% of value added, one of the highest levels in Europe) and its exposure to international competition. Furthermore, the delay in modernising electricity infrastructure (only 22.6% of the high-voltage lines planned for 2025 had actually been completed by that date) is causing bottlenecks between the production areas in the north and the consumption centres in the south. As a result, the costs of accessing services have increased fivefold over 10 years (rising from EUR 1 bn in 2014 to EUR 5.2 bn in 2024[13]). At the same time, as we have already seen, taxation and grid charges are hitting industry hard, with levies on large consumers far exceeding the European average despite some support mechanisms being put in place for the most electricity-intensive companies (such as the Bandlastprivileg measure to reduce grid tariffs). As a result, German industrial production has suffered in particular due to rising energy prices in recent years, including electricity, with electricity-intensive industries being especially affected (Chart 8).
In order to cope with these higher electricity costs than the European average, Germany has been using European support schemes to reduce the cost of electricity for businesses, particularly since the Merz government took office in May 2025. The main scheme — the Industriestrompreis[14], made possible by the CISAF — has been approved by the European Commission for the 2026–2028 period. While it is less beneficial than the indirect carbon cost (ICC) offsetting included in electricity prices[15], it has a broader scope, meaning that businesses ineligible for the ICC can benefit from it. articles.title: European Regulation of Personal Data Protection - Вокс Україна
articles.summary: European Regulation of Personal Data Protection  Вокс Україна
articles.full_text:
When you shop online, post on social media, or just go for a walk with a phone in your pocket, you leave a digital footprint wherever you go.
Companies such as Google can profit from the data you generate in this way, for example, by showing you advertisements for products or services similar to those you have searched for (and receiving payment from providers of those products or services). Therefore, the well-known saying that “data is the new oil” is justified: while in 2008 two of the five largest companies in the world were in the oil industry, by 2018 all five were data-related companies.
Since data generates profits, several questions arise: Who owns it? How can owners control their data? How can others use it? These and other questions are addressed by a number of EU regulations and directives (see box). The EU currently has the most advanced regulatory framework in this area, which other countries use as a model. Companies based outside the EU that process EU residents’ data must comply with these rules too. To facilitate international cooperation for European companies, the European Commission can recognise countries and organisations as providing a level of personal data protection equivalent to that of the EU (currently 16 jurisdictions and organisations, including Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay). Companies and organisations covered by these decisions do not need additional authorisations or separate contracts to exchange data with EU companies.
European legislation has two main objectives: to create a single EU market for data open to companies and organisations from other countries, and to protect property rights of individuals over their personal data. Thus, individuals should be able to allow or prohibit the processing of their data, modify or delete it, transfer it to another platform etc.
As part of its EU accession process, Ukraine will need to incorporate the legislation listed in the box, along with any other legislation the EU may adopt to protect personal data, into its national legal framework and establish the necessary supporting infrastructure.
On 15 June 2026, Ukraine opened the first cluster of EU accession negotiations. This cluster includes Chapter 23, “Judiciary and Fundamental Rights”, and Chapter 24, “Justice, Freedom and Security”. Among other, the document calls for the full alignment of Ukrainian legislation with the EU”s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Two draft laws needed to achieve this — No. 8153 on personal data protection, which would replace the existing law, and No. 6177 on establishing a National Commission for Personal Data Protection — have been pending in Parliament for several years. What do these draft laws propose and what will change once Ukraine complies with the GDPR?
EU legislation regulating the data market and protecting personal data
Convention 108+ on data protection (2018) is a cornerstone convention that establishes the principles of data protection and provides the basis for other legislation. To date, 55 countries, including Ukraine, have signed the Convention.
The General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or GDPR) came into force in 2018. It replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC), whose provisions had become outdated in light of technological developments.
The following legislative acts supplement the GDPR or regulate specific aspects of it.
The Digital Services Act (2022) aims to create a safer online environment for individuals and businesses. It prohibits online platforms from displaying targeted advertising to children or targeting ads based on sensitive personal data, such as race, religion or sexual orientation. Advertisements must be clearly labelled, and users must be able to identify who is behind them.
The Digital Markets Act (2022) aims to make digital markets more competitive. To this end, it prohibits operators acting as “gatekeepers” from sharing personal data between their platforms without users” consent (for example, when you use your Google account to log in to LinkedIn, you must authorise the first platform to share your data with the second one).
The AI Act (2024) sets rules for data protection and processing in areas where AI is used, such as facial or voice recognition systems.
The Platform Work Directive (2024) regulates the processing of personal data by platforms that connect freelancers with employers, such as Uber or Kabanchik.
The Political Advertising Regulation (2024) prohibits targeting political advertisements at minors and using certain categories of personal data for such targeting, including ethnic or racial origin, political opinions and health information.
The European Digital Identity Regulation (2024) provides the framework for creating the European Digital Identity Wallet, a system similar to Ukraine”s Diia that allows individuals to verify their identity and store and sign digital documents. Once the wallet is fully rolled out (planned by the end of 2027), individuals will have full control over their personal data.
The ePrivacy Directive (2002), which remains in force, regulates aspects of users” digital footprints online, including cookies, mailing list subscriptions and spam. Attempts to replace it with a modern ePrivacy Regulation have so far been unsuccessful.
The Interoperable Europe Act (2022) aims to make digital public services across the EU interoperable (for example, enabling individuals to apply for a passport, complete tax forms and apply for benefits through a single platform rather than through the websites of individual government agencies).
Like most EU legislation, the GDPR (hereafter, the Regulation) is based on the principle of balancing different objectives and interests of different parties. For example, individuals have the right to be forgotten, but not when exercising that right would conflict with important public interests. Similarly, a data controller must inform data subjects of a change in the purpose of processing their data, unless doing so would require too much resources. The Regulation therefore leaves considerable room for discretion of stakeholders. It frequently uses terms such as “reasonable” or “sufficient” measures, leaving those involved in data processing and its regulation to determine what these terms mean in practice.
Although the Regulation is directly applicable, many of its provisions are vaguely worded (for example, requiring “reasonable measures”). Its implementation therefore relies on a functioning institutional framework (Figure 1) and an effective judicial system, both of which are expected to interpret and supplement its provisions and, where necessary, propose amendments if ambiguities or disputes arise during implementation (for example, the European Court of Human Rights provides a range of clarifications related to the Regulation based on its cases).
*Under the current law, these are defined as data owners. **Under the current law, these are defined as data administrators. However, it is not always possible to determine with certainty whether a particular legal entity is a data controller, a data processor, or both. In such cases, individuals may seek clarification from the national regulator, the European Data Protection Board or, in the case of EU institutions, the European Data Protection Supervisor.
What does the GDPR regulate?
The Regulation governs the processing of personal data of living natural persons (Ukraine’s current law on personal data protection also covers legal entities and sole proprietors). The GDPR primarily concerns data processing by commercial and non-governmental organisations, since it does not apply to data processing for the purposes of foreign policy and national security, criminal law or the provision of public services (these are subject to separate legislation, such as Directive 2016/680 on the protection of personal data in criminal proceedings).
Some provisions of the Regulation govern data processing for scientific and historical purposes (research and archiving), but the Regulation does not apply to the data of deceased persons (which is governed by national legislation). The Regulation also calls for broad interpretation of freedom of expression recognising its importance to democracy. Its provisions should therefore not be applied where they would impede freedom of expression and information, including journalistic and scientific activities or literary and artistic expression (although individual countries elaborate on these provisions in different ways).
How do individuals exercise ownership of their personal data?
First, individuals must provide active informed consent on processing of their data (consent by default, which is permitted under current Ukrainian law, is not allowed under the GDPR). A company that collects and/or processes data must provide individuals with full information about how their data will be used, and they must consent to that use verbally or in writing (for example, by ticking a box on a form). The Regulation emphasises that this information must be provided in clear, plain language (although research has shown that in reality it is rarely the case).
Individuals may refuse to consent to the processing of their data, and this should not prevent them from receiving a service. However, when someone enters into a contract for a particular service, they also agree to the processing of the data necessary to provide it (the Regulation establishes the de minimis principle, meaning that controllers should collect only the data they need). For example, when someone places an order with an online shop, the retailer needs their name, telephone number and delivery address. A customer may refuse to provide other information, such as their date of birth or marital status, and this should not lead to refusing delivery. Fabio Panetta spoke in Turin and described recent debt market moves as global, with the United States at the epicenter. He said growth and inflation in the United States have exceeded expectations, while growth in Europe is weaker.
