articles.title: Estonia on the edge as Russia-NATO tensions rise - The Hindu
articles.summary: Estonia on the edge as Russia-NATO tensions rise  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
On October 12, NATO’s top military commander issued a stark warning to Russia. General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said that if Moscow were “foolish enough” to attack an alliance territory, NATO would destroy “anything and everything” involved in the attack.
His remarks came at a time of rising tensions between Russia and European nations. And one country that finds itself under pressure on the hot Russia-NATO border is the tiny Estonia.
When the U.S., Canada, and 10 other European nations came together in 1949, in the early phase of the Cold War, to form the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), they had a clear goal. As Lord Hastings Lionel Ismay, the alliance’s first Secretary General, famously put it, the purpose was to “keep the Soviet Union out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”
Throughout the Cold War, NATO had been the primary military bulwark against Soviet power in Europe. After the disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia fell into a phase of strategic retreat, while NATO expanded towards Eastern Europe. This set the stage for renewed tensions once Russia started reasserting itself in the region.
The situation became even more complicated after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine was offered NATO membership in 2018, but it never became a member. So it’s not covered by NATO’s Article 5 collective defence, but in its war with Russia, Kyiv is getting military support from NATO members.
The war has also prompted European states lately to raise concerns over Russia’s grey-zone activities. These include cyberattacks, sabotage, disinformation, and electronic interference.
A sensitive border city
Grey-zone activities are designed to put pressure on a country without necessarily triggering an open military conflict. Moscow has denied these allegations.
These concerns have become particularly important in the Baltic region, where fears are growing that Russia could attempt to spread instability beyond Ukraine without launching a full-scale invasion of another European country. This leaves Estoinia in a vulnerable position. Located in northeastern Europe, Estonia, formerly part of the Soviet Union, shares border with Russia and sits along NATO’s eastern flank. The country became independent after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
It joined NATO in 2004, upsetting Moscow.
A small country bordering the Baltic Sea to its west and Russia to its east, Estonia sits in an unenviable location. Its proximity to Russian territory means that any military movements, border incidents, and developments in the surrounding region can have immediate consequences for its national security. Estonia is not alone in facing these challenges. Latvia and Lithuania also sit on NATO’s eastern flank, while Finland, a recent NATO member, shares a long land border with Russia.
For a country of around 1.3 million people, covering approximately 45,000 sq. km, Estonia risks getting caught between Russia and NATO is the crisis escales into conflict.
According to a report in the Financial Times, Russian state media has always portrayed Estonia as a hostile, “Russophobic” country seeking confrontation with Moscow. Russian officials have issued warnings about NATO’s military presence in the Baltic region.
One location attracting particular attention is Narva, an Estonian city on the Russian border, separated from the Russian city of Ivangorod by the Narva River. Its geographical position makes it important to Estonia’s border security. The city also has a predominantly Russian-speaking population.
Estonian officials fear that Moscow could attempt to exploit local tensions or use disinformation to create pressure on the country. The question for Estonia now is how to prepare for the possibility of the worst.
‘Active’ defence strategy
The Estonian government introduced the concept of “active defence” into its national security planning in 2026.
Since then, the country’s small military has begun a major reorganisation, shifting away from a strategy that could allow Russian forces to advance into Estonian territory before a counter-attack.
From Tapa, one of Estonia’s main military bases, troops are being redeployed further east, closer to the Russian border.
A new military facility is being developed in Jõhvi, while another base is being built in Narva itself.
According to the Financial Times, the planned Narva facility is designed to house around 200 soldiers, with space for up to 1,000 during a crisis.
Estonia has also begun shifting towards a strategy designed to prevent an adversary from gaining territory in the first place.
Rather than relying on a later counter-attack, its forces would attempt to engage Russian troops from the beginning of an invasion while using longer-range weapons to strike military targets behind the front line.
Col. Tarmo Kundla, commander of the Estonian First Brigade, has explained the thinking behind this approach. In simple terms, he said, Estonia wants to stop an invading force from gaining ground rather than allowing it to advance and then attempting to take back the territory later (a lesson learnt from the war in Ukraine).
Adding to this is Estonia’s military spending and weapons purchases. Estonia’s defence spending is set to rise by 42% in 2026, reaching €2.4 billion, or around 5.4% of its GDP.
The country has also signed contracts to acquire nine U.S.-made HIMARS rocket launcher systems and nine South Korean Chunmoo systems. This includes M57 ballistic missiles with a reported range of up to 300 km. This is significant because St. Petersburg, one of Russia’s largest cities, lies approximately 260 km from Estonia.
Depending on the weapon used and the target involved, these systems could put military targets deep inside Russian territory within striking distance. Coming to Estonia’s manpower, the country has a trained reserve force of up to 2,30,000 people, while its permanent standing forces comprise around 4,200 personnel.
Estonia cannot defend itself entirely alone. The country does not have its own conventional combat air force and relies on NATO allies for air policing and the wider protection of its skies. Hence, it cannot be separated from the role of NATO in its military preparations.
The U.K. has maintained a military presence in Estonia as part of NATO’s forward defence. The Financial Times reports that Britain has committed to increasing its deployment from around 800 to 1,200 troops by April 2027. These deployments are intended to strengthen deterrence by making clear that an attack on Estonia could involve forces from other NATO members from the beginning of the conflict.
Estonian officials have expressed concerns about the possibility of a future conflict, but they are also preparing for the risk of a smaller attack designed to test the alliance’s response.
“I’m not sure if we can deter the mad person. What we have to do is to prepare,” said Gen. Martin Herem, former Commander of Estonian Defence Forces and current Defence Minister, earlier this month. “And that’s the only thing. We have to prepare very seriously [for an attack], and in doing so, we may prevent it.”
(Smriti Sudesh is a postgraduate student at SOAS University of London)

articles.title: WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond  Al JazeeraUK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks  BBCOperational update 20 October – UK military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia  GOV.UKUK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks  The GuardianDonald Trump’s lethal indifference has dragged us to the brink of disaster in the Gulf  The Independent
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has announced it will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The jets will play a “defensive role”, the British Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that they will not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group.
The move comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone attacks against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.
The UK’s decision to send jets to assist Saudi Arabia marks just the latest chapter in a partnership that stretches back more than a century, to a treaty signed during the First World War, years before the Saudi kingdom was founded.
So what is the UK sending, and how did the two countries become so closely bound?
Here’s what you need to know:
What is the UK sending?
Fighter jets, an A400M transport aircraft and advisers.
The ministry said it was also extending air-to-air refuelling, which it previously agreed to provide for Saudi air operations, including those to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen.
How far back does the UK-Saudi relationship go?
To the First World War.
In December 1915, Sir Percy Cox, a senior British official in the Gulf, concluded the Treaty of Darin with King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, then ruler of Nejd in central Arabia, according to India Office records held by the UK’s National Archives.
In return, he allied with Britain against the Ottoman Empire, and Britain backed him with cash and weapons.
In May 1927, Britain signed a new treaty with him at Jeddah, according to an India Office memorandum.
King Abdulaziz founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.
When did UK-Saudi arms deals begin?
In the 1960s.
In May 1966, Saudi Arabia signed contracts to buy 40 Lightning fighter jets and 25 jet trainers from the British Aircraft Corporation, along with a radar system, according to a US Department of State memo from the time.
Even then, Yemen was part of the picture.
In 1962, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen was overthrown in a military coup and the Yemen Arab Republic was established. Egypt sent troops to back the republican government, while Saudi Arabia and Jordan armed and funded royalist forces trying to restore the Imam. By 1966, the civil war had reached a stalemate.
Meanwhile, Britain was facing rebellion from Soviet- and Egypt-backed nationalist groups over its control of Aden and southern Yemen. Britain ultimately withdrew in 1967.
In 1966, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Prince Sultan, asked the UK to supply an RAF fighter squadron to fly under Saudi colours if fighting resumed in Yemen, according to declassified US State Department records.
Britain instead offered fighter jets flown by British pilots, and said it was ready to send an RAF squadron of Lightning interceptors for a short period if required.
In the end, Saudi Arabia accepted the jets and civilian pilots, and the RAF squadron was not needed, the records show.
BAE Systems, then the British Aircraft Corporation, says its ties with Saudi Arabia date back to 1966, and in 1973, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding naming the company as prime contractor.
1980s and the Al-Yamamah deal
In 1985, the two governments signed an oil-for-arms agreement, known as Al-Yamamah, for Tornado and Hawk jets.
The Reuters news agency has described the Al-Yamamah deals as the largest export contracts in British history.
Saudi Arabia set aside up to 600,000 barrels of oil a day to pay for Tornado jets and other equipment.
The UK’s Serious Fraud Office investigated corruption allegations linked to the deal from 2004, but dropped the inquiry in December 2006, according to a House of Lords judgement.
The attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, cited the need to safeguard national security.
Has Britain fought from Saudi soil before?
Yes.
When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, King Fahd of Saudi Arabia asked friendly governments for help.
On August 11, 12 RAF Tornado fighters flew from Akrotiri in Cyprus to Dhahran in Saudi Arabia, according to the RAF Museum.
Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990, and at Dhahran in January 1991, the museum’s records show.
During the war, then-Defence Secretary Tom King told Parliament that Saudi Arabia had provided the UK with host-nation support.
He also reported that a Tornado based in the kingdom had gone missing, the fourth lost in enemy action.
British aircraft then patrolled a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, alongside United States and French jets, flying from Saudi bases until 2003, according to the US Air Force.
Where do the Typhoons come in?
In September 2007, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons from Britain, the UK MoD said at the time. The jets were to replace Tornadoes and other aircraft in the Saudi air force.
The deal was worth 4.43 billion pounds (then about $8.9bn).
BAE Systems, which builds the jets, called it the Salam Project.
Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990 and at Dhahran in January 1991.
In March 2018, during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to London, the UK signed a memorandum of intent with Saudi Arabia to finalise the purchase of 48 more Typhoons, BAE Systems said in a statement to the London Stock Exchange.
But the deal stalled.
Germany, which helps build the Typhoon and has a veto over its exports, halted arms sales to Saudi Arabia after the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a columnist for The Washington Post who wrote critically of the crown prince and his policies, in 2018.
Berlin dropped its objection in January 2024, with then-Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock saying the Middle East had become a completely different place since October 7, 2023, when southern Israel was attacked by Hamas and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza.
BAE said that year it was supporting the UK government in discussions with Saudi Arabia.
What about Yemen?
In June 2019, five years after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, triggering a brutal civil war, the UK’s Court of Appeal ruled that the government had acted unlawfully by licensing arms sales to Saudi Arabia for possible use in Yemen without assessing whether past incidents had breached international humanitarian law.
New licences were halted. In July 2020, then-Trade Secretary Liz Truss told Parliament they would resume, saying there was not a clear risk the arms would be used in a serious violation of the law.
The UK has also struck the Houthis directly. RAF Typhoons joined US attacks on Yemen in 2024 following Houthi attacks on Israel-linked Red Sea shipping in response to the bombardment of Gaza, according to the MoD.
Then, in September this year, Britain sent a Voyager tanker to assist Saudi Arabia with air-to-air refuelling of fighter jets. The planes it refuels are British-built Typhoons flown by the Saudi air force.

articles.title: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing  The GuardianRegulators unveil plans to simplify Senior Manager and Certification Regime  Bank of EnglandUK waters down ‘fit and proper’ rules set up to hold bankers to account  Financial TimesUK financial regulators propose easing vetting rules for finance employees  ReutersUK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing.
The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks.
The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs.
This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures that came into force in the mid-2010s, in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash.
The senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, it was later expanded to cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds.
It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helped lift the cap on banker bonuses, which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary.
The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls.
Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers.
The regulators said removing these “unnecessary burdens” would save businesses about £2bn over 10 years while cutting the Bank of England’s and FCA’s costs by £11.5m and £229m each year, respectively.
The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. They said in a joint statement that the “high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers”.

Citi sees more upside risk for oil prices despite recovering Middle Eastern crude exports, a considerably less bearish assessment from the bank that predicted $60-to-$65 Brent by year-end just three months ago.
Brent December futures traded at $111.70 on Thursday, up $2.88, or 2.65%, after touching $112.68 earlier in the session.
The problem, Citi says, is that getting crude out of the Gulf and getting it to buyers at a reasonable cost are two different things.
More than 1 million barrels per day of Gulf crude was transferred between vessels in September, representing about 7.5% of regional exports. Before the U.S.-Iran war, these transfers were virtually nonexistent.
Freight rates for very large crude carriers traveling from the Gulf to China recently approached $250 per metric ton, or roughly $35 per barrel, Citi estimates. That's more than 20 times the previous decade's average.
Excluding Iran, Gulf crude exports recovered to more than 81% of prewar levels in September, aided by increased Saudi shipments. Iran's own exports have fallen to zero under a U.S. blockade.
Before the war began in February, the Strait of Hormuz handled about one-fifth of the world's oil and LNG supplies.
Citi has had to rethink its oil market outlook repeatedly. In July, it urged investors to sell summer rallies and predicted Brent would fall to $60-$65 by year-end as Hormuz shipping normalized.
In August, Citi raised its third-quarter Brent forecast from $75 to $80 but left its fourth-quarter call at $70 and its 2027 forecast at $65. Brent was trading at $83.11 when Citi issued that revision.
The bank offered no new price target in Thursday's assessment. Instead, it warned that the recovery in Gulf exports has been a recovery in volumes, not shipping efficiency.
Buyers are receiving more crude, but the added transfers and soaring freight costs are keeping delivered supplies expensive.

Germany is the target of "intensive" espionage activity, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said after a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia.
Officials said the suspect, named as Vadym Y., had allegedly collected military-related intelligence from Germany.
Merz called the uncovering of the case a "success", but warned "let us not delude ourselves - the activities of Russian intelligence services in Germany remain at a consistently high level".
Several people alleged to be acting on behalf of Russia and other foreign powers have been arrested in Germany this year. Germany has been one of the leading European suppliers of weapons to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The German Federal Prosecutor General's Office said on Thursday that Vadym Y., as he was identified under German privacy law, had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025.
It also said the Ukrainian man had collected information including "on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition, and explosives".
He is due to appear before an investigating judge on Friday.
In January, a woman was arrested in Berlin suspected of gathering information for an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy.
Other arrests this year included a Romanian woman and a Ukrainian man accused of spying on an individual supplying drones from Germany to Ukraine, according to the prosecutor's office.

articles.title: Brazil: Brazil's Runoff: Why a Bolsonaro Win Would Shake Europe's Trade Plans - Friedrich Naumann Foundation
articles.summary: Brazil: Brazil's Runoff: Why a Bolsonaro Win Would Shake Europe's Trade Plans  Friedrich Naumann Foundation
articles.full_text:
Why Brazil's Presidential Election Is Geopolitically Crucial for Europe
      
It is more than just a symbolic image. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro stands in the Oval Office of the White House. The 45-year-old wears a yellow-and-green-striped tie—the colors of Brazil—and stares intently into the camera. Seated at the desk in front of him, United States of America, President Donald Trump smiles broadly. The photo was taken on May 26 of this year. Although it was already clear by then that the eldest son of imprisoned former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro intended to run in the presidential election, he had not yet officially announced his candidacy. Nevertheless, he was certain of Trump’s support.
Just a few weeks earlier, the left-leaning incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had met with the USA president at the White House. The photos from that visit tell a different story. The two heads of state are seated across from each other in armchairs, Trump leaning forward and Lula gesturing wildly with his legs crossed. Lula, who is now campaigning for a fourth term, wanted to demonstrate strength on equal footing and project Brazil’s newfound foreign policy confidence to the world.
When Bolsonaro Jr. and Lula face off in the presidential runoff on October 25, it will not merely be a clash between two camps that have been at odds for nearly a decade. The USA is acting as a powerful player behind the scenes. Trump sees an opportunity to expand his strategic influence in Latin America.
In recent months, conservative politicians who favor closer ties with the major partner to the north have won every election in Latin America. So far, Brazil—the region’s most important economy—has been the exception. A victory for Bolsonaro Jr. in the runoff would therefore also be a victory for Trump. In the first round of the presidential election on October 4, the right-wing conservative politician led Lula by about three percentage points.
As expected, foreign policy issues are not at the center of the election campaign. Nevertheless, this election also involves a fundamental decision: How should Brazil position itself vis-à-vis the USA in the future?
A one-sided alignment with Washington would be a risk for Bolsonaro
The trade conflict that Trump instigated last year was sparked by Jair Bolsonaro’s sentencing to 27 years in prison for an attempted coup. Trump wielded the tariff stick and imposed additional duties on Brazilian exports. Behind this was an overt threat to Lula’s left-leaning government.
Most recently, in July, Trump imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods. Products such as beef and coffee were exempt. In doing so, the USA president spared powerful agricultural producers, who are key supporters of Bolsonaro Jr. Although Trump is not openly interfering in the Brazilian election campaign, he is nonetheless exerting influence through statements supporting Bolsonaro and his tariff policy.
While the USA. is aggressively pursuing its power politics, Europe remains in a wait-and-see mode. It is too uncertain how Bolsonaro Jr. will position himself on foreign policy as a potential new president. The only certainty is that ties with the USA are likely to grow closer. That would mark a break from the course of “active non-alignment” pursued by Lula.
In his campaign platform, Bolsonaro Jr. presents himself as moderate and avoids radical rhetoric. On foreign policy issues, however, he remains vague, and his statements are at times contradictory. This is evident in the EU-Mercosur agreement, the free trade initiative between Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay and the European Union.
Bolsonaro Jr. speaks of freeing Brazil “from the shackles” of the Mercosur agreement and relying more on bilateral treaties. He said he would “aggressively” seek new agreements. It remains unclear whether he is aiming for a complete withdrawal from the Mercosur agreement, a suspension, or renegotiations in certain areas, such as environmental protection requirements.
Bolsonaro Questions the EU-Mercosur Agreement
According to his own statements, one of his first actions will be to conclude a bilateral free trade agreement with the USA modeled after Argentina’s. This would grant the United States privileged market access. European suppliers would be left behind.
The stakes are high for the EU. After more than 25 rounds of negotiations, the agreement with the Mercosur countries was finally brought across the finish line this year—at least in terms of provisional implementation. Lula played a decisive role in this. It is his greatest foreign policy triumph.
However, even a slight weakening of the free trade agreement would be disastrous for Europe. This is because many EU countries, led by Germany, are struggling with sluggish growth and are counting on new markets in Brazil. At the same time, they are seeking to reduce their economic dependencies. Brazil possesses the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth elements, has numerous offshore oil reserves that have not yet been developed, and intends to expand the mining of iron ore and critical raw materials.
Bolsonaro has also made an announcement regarding security policy that is likely to be noted with interest in Europe. He intends to join the “Shield of the Americas” security initiative, which was founded by Trump about eight months ago. The pact, which currently includes 19 Latin American countries, aims to combat cross-border drug trafficking and organized crime.
Lula Defends Multilateralism and Neutrality
As the USA assumes a leading role in the alliance, Trump’s influence in the region is growing. The two largest countries in Latin America, Brazil and Mexico, are currently led by center-left governments and have not yet joined the alliance. They fear that Washington could expand its claim to power in the region.
Bolsonaro Jr. also supports Trump’s decision to designate Brazil’s two largest criminal organizations, the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital) and Comando Vermelho, as terrorist organizations. This marks another break with Lula’s foreign policy, as his administration had unsuccessfully argued against the move, citing Brazil’s sovereignty. Such a designation of criminal organizations gives the USA a stronger legal basis to crack down on the cartels—including through operations on Brazilian soil.
These examples show that the Brazilian presidential election has significance far beyond the country’s borders. A government under Lula would adhere to the traditional principles of Brazilian foreign policy: autonomy, multilateralism, and cooperation with various partners.
Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has announced a geopolitical reorientation. He would shift the focus toward the USA, while Europe would become less important. Efforts to strengthen partnerships and economic ties could thus suffer significant setbacks.
However, a foreign policy orientation that is one-sidedly aligned with the USA would also be risky for Bolsonaro Jr. Should he align himself closely with the White House, he could face resistance from within his own ranks. Political scientist Octavio Amorim Neto of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo anticipates conflicts with segments of the economic elite, nationalist forces within the armed forces, and major media conglomerates. He attributes this to economic interests and concerns that Brazil might sacrifice some of its autonomy if it were to form ties with Washington that are too close.
Uncertain Future for Brazil’s BRICS Membership
Bolsonaro Jr. has explicitly called into question not only the future of the Mercosur agreement but also Brazil’s BRICS membership. On his first day as president, he said in a podcast that he would examine whether Brazil should remain in an alliance that is ideologically driven and provokes the USA
Under the Lula administration, Brazil has advocated for a pragmatic and open approach to the alliance, which is anything but homogeneous. The BRICS should explicitly not be viewed as an anti-Western alliance, but rather as a means of pooling the political and economic interests of its member states. In 2025, Brazil hosted the BRICS summit. China, Russia, India, and Brazil are founding members of the alliance, which has since expanded.
In an increasingly multipolar world marked by growing tensions and conflicts, the BRICS group could continue to gain in importance. Brazil’s withdrawal would not only weaken the alliance; the South American country would also lose international influence and jeopardize its self-proclaimed role as a mediator between different centers of power.
Under Lula, Brazil has increasingly sought closer ties with Europe. Its support for the Mercosur agreement is one example of this. Further evidence is the decision not to join China’s “Belt and Road” initiative. In doing so, Brazil is attempting to limit its dependence on China and preserve its autonomy.
Brazil Remains a Key Geopolitical Player
With its renewed engagement in Latin America, the United States aims above all to curb China’s influence in the region—both economically and politically. But the groundwork has already been laid. China is by far Brazil’s largest trading partner, ahead of the USA Brazil is the world’s leading supplier of agricultural products to China, such as soybeans, beef, sugar, and corn. The leader of Europe’s biggest economy, who is set to travel next week to Singapore, Japan and South Korea, criticised Chinese industrial overcapacities, subsidies for products and export advantages that he said came from an artificially cheap currency.
“We want to have fair trade with China in our joint and mutual interest. That is our goal,” Merz said at a Berlin conference.
“But at the same time, we have to be ready to defend ourselves, to defend our industry.”
Germany – home to industrial giants in the auto, chemicals and electronics sectors – long prided itself on a massive trade surplus with the rest of the world, including booming sales to China.
That has turned in recent years, however, as Chinese firms have become increasingly competitive and German exporters have been hit by rising production costs and US tariffs.
In recent months, EU leaders including Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have seriously weighed new policy moves to protect EU-based industry from Chinese competition.
Merz said recent talks by EU officials with China had made some progress, including an agreement to reduce the number of cars exported to the European market.
He said the moves “are not the beginning of a trade war with China”.
“But we will also protect our industry with a new set of EU trade defence instruments, because in sustainable trade relations, one side shouldn’t profit at the expense of the other,” Merz said.
“Germany, France and the entire EU (have) now come to the point where they are ready to defend their interests and that’s what we are doing,” he said.
Merz noted that China’s total trade surplus with the EU was well over €300 billion (US$337 billion) each year.
He said some of China’s success was due to strong new companies and excellent research, adding that “we have to respect that”.
He also acknowledged that structural problems in Europe had created problems for the German economy and weighed on exports.
“But this is also due to overcapacities, high subsidies on the automotive sector and others and… an artificially under-valued currency” in China, Merz added. “This has to be addressed.”
While Merz is travelling elsewhere in Asia next week, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who holds a largely ceremonial post, will visit China next week.
Steinmeier’s office said he plans to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the first visit to China by a German president since 2018.

A cancer vaccine being developed by Merck and Moderna significantly reduced melanoma deaths compared to conventional treatments, according to data released on Thursday, though an online leak of the study prompted chaotic trading in their shares.
Although the results were in line with analysts’ expectations, Moderna’s shares sank about 18 per cent. The data was not scheduled to be published until Saturday but the companies released it after details of the trial results leaked out.
The results follow an August announcement from Merck and Moderna that said messenger RNA technology (mRNA) combined with conventional melanoma treatments proved successful in stopping cancer from returning and spreading in patients whose melanomas had been removed. Moderna’s shares more than doubled after the announcement; the Boston-based biotech remains the best performer in the S&P 500 index this year despite Thursday’s drop.
The latest trial results provided more information, specifically about the timing for a patient’s survival. After six months, the combination of mRNA and Merck’s cancer-killing drug Keytruda reduced the risk of tumour recurrence or death by 58 per cent, the companies said.
The timing of patients’ recurrence-free survival was in line with analysts’ estimates but failed to significantly improve upon Wall Street’s expectations.
The reduction in cancer recurrences and death is meaningful, said Evan Seigerman, analyst at BMO Capital Markets. The share price reaction “likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment of the efficacy of the combo therapy”, he said.

Analysts said it remains uncertain how the melanoma results can be applied to other cancers. Merck and Moderna are also testing their therapies in bladder, lung and other cancers.

articles.title: EU looks to Vietnam for trade — and turns a blind eye to rights abuses - DW.com
articles.summary: EU looks to Vietnam for trade — and turns a blind eye to rights abuses  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.
The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.
Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.
"This is a win-win for both sides," he said. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."
Vietnam-EU ties deepen
Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.
Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.
"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he said, referring to the European Union's efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.
Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.
Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record
The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.
Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.
In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.
When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.
These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.
Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.
"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.
Benefits 'distributed unevenly'
There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.
Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.
Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.
"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.
"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.
Better for EU?
Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.
Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.
The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.
This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.
Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.
"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.
The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.
"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.
"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.
For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.
Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

articles.summary: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots  BBCAngry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases  The GuardianFrance’s devastation and its aftermath  The EconomistFrance's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest  ReutersFrance bans ‘illegitimate’ protests this weekend after riots  The Times
articles.full_text:
Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend.
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.
France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.
Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.
The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses.
The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT).
Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced.
"When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.

articles.title: Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl - City AM
articles.summary: Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl  City AMAldi and Lidl will be subject to same rules as major supermarkets  GOV.UKCMA: Aldi and Lidl will face same land rules as other supermarkets  The GrocerOnly 26 sites on the UK market could provide Aldi or Lidl a new location  The GrocerAldi and Lidl Reach a New Milestone in the UK Grocery Market  EasternEye
articles.full_text:
Supermarket giants, including Waitrose and Morrisons, have welcomed the competition watchdog’s decision to crack down on Aldi and Lidl.
Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” loophole to block rivals from opening nearby.
However, the competition regulator is now set to force the two grocers to comply.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on Thursday confirmed its provisional decision to extend the Controlled Land Order to cover Aldi and Lidl.
The pair had previously been excluded from the rules because they were classed as “limited assortment discounters”. But the CMA has said it will now categorise the two firms as “large grocery retailers” because of their rapid expansion in recent years.
Lidl and Aldi will join Asda, Co-op, Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose in being blocked from using these land laws to gain an advantage over their rivals.
Budget supermarket Iceland, which is not covered by the land order, welcomed the CMA’s provisional decision.
In a letter to the regulator, published on Thursday, the company said existing rules allowed Aldi and Lidl to “deploy problematic land arrangements […] at scale and in a way that could have a material adverse impact on competition for groceries across the UK market”.
Though the two German discounters occupied a relatively small part of the UK’s grocery market when the Controlled Land Order was set up, the firms “now each exert a significant and compelling degree of competitive influence in the UK grocery market,” Iceland said.
Lidl and Aldi ‘shielded from competition’
Grocers Morrisons, Waitrose and Iceland each wrote to the CMA, expressing concerns that Lidl and Aldi are preparing to expand further in the UK, citing plans to reach 1,500 stores each.
Aldi and Lidl have previously claimed they should not be classed as large grocery retailers because they offer fewer products than their rivals.
But Morrisons told the CMA that both supermarket chains “publicly market their product range as being suitable for a full weekly shop” and pose “intense competition” even in the categories they claim to be weak in.
A Waitrose spokesperson wrote to the regulator, warning that it had seen “first hand” Lidl’s use of the land order to “restrict the ability of other grocery retailers to open new stores and shield Lidl from local competition”.
The up-market grocer said the CMA should impose its rulings as soon as possible. “It is important that these decisions are taken without further delay to ensure there is equal opportunity in the competition between LGRs and Aldi and Lidl to secure further sites for grocery retail.”
Juliette Enser, executive director for competition enforcement at the regulator, said the new rules will “help level the playing field and make sure shoppers get the best choice of products and prices in their area”.
Responding to the CMA’s provisional ruling in August, Lidl and Aldi said the crackdown would not slow their plans to expand rapidly in the UK.
Commenting on the decision, an Aldi spokesperson said: “We remain firmly committed to opening hundreds of new stores across the country, bringing Aldi’s unbeatable value and award-winning quality to even more customers.
A Lidl spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we have always welcomed and embraced competition within the market, and our focus remains on continuing to open new stores and bringing our high-quality, lowest-priced groceries to even more communities.”

articles.title: Domestic companies need strategic approach to tap India-Europe FTA gains: FICCI - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Domestic companies need strategic approach to tap India-Europe FTA gains: FICCI  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
FICCI says MSMEs must upgrade product quality, meet European sustainability standards and integrate into regional supply chains to convert the India-EU free trade agreement into sustained export growth.
FICCI Secretary General Anant Swarup said the real challenge would be to convert improved market access into sustained market penetration.
He said that although the agreement, concluded in January, presents an unprecedented opportunity for Indian MSMEs to expand their presence in the European market, tariff concessions alone will not translate into higher exports.
Swarup is accompanying Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who is on a two-day visit here to boost trade and investment ties between India and Germany, its largest EU trading partner.
He said that MSMEs can also benefit by becoming suppliers to larger Indian and European companies, particularly in sectors such as textiles, leather, engineering components, chemicals and processed foods.
He noted that compliance with European standards will remain one of the most critical determinants of export success.
EU requirements relating to product safety, technical standards, sustainability, traceability and carbon emissions can be particularly challenging for smaller enterprises, he said, adding the EU's evolving regulatory framework, including CBAM (carbon border adjustment mechanism) and other sustainability-related requirements, will require Indian businesses to invest in cleaner technologies, certification and compliance systems.
Three areas of support will be particularly important: information and market intelligence, testing and certification infrastructure, and technology and financial support, he said.
He elaborated that industry needs practical, product-specific guidance on tariff concessions, rules of origin, regulatory requirements and export opportunities.
Dedicated FTA helpdesks, sector-specific advisory services and buyer-seller platforms can bridge this information gap.
"India must expand internationally accredited testing laboratories and certification facilities, particularly in major export clusters. Greater cooperation between Indian and European conformity assessment bodies can help reduce duplication, costs and delays," the Secretary General said.
MSMEs will need access to affordable finance, modern technology, digital traceability systems and support for meeting environmental and sustainability standards.
He added that shared facilities and targeted technology-upgradation programmes can make these investments more affordable.
"The FTA provides an institutional framework for regulatory dialogue and cooperation. This should be actively leveraged to address technical barriers, improve transparency and facilitate greater recognition of testing and certification systems wherever feasible," Swarup said.
He also said that Indian firms should look at the FTA beyond immediate tariff benefits as it can catalyse European investment into India, encourage technology partnerships, strengthen integration into global value chains and support diversification of our export markets.
"The real opportunity is not simply to export more to Europe, but to position India as a trusted manufacturing and services partner in European supply chains. This can deliver sustained gains in investment, production, employment and technological capabilities," he added.
India and the EU announced the conclusion of negotiations for the free trade agreement on January 27.
It is expected to be signed in December this year and may come into force next year.
India's exports to EU countries dipped by 4.57 per cent to $72.4 billion in 2025-26 from $75.85 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 17 per cent of India's total merchandise shipments in the last fiscal.
Imports, on the other hand, rose by 9 per cent to $66.18 billion in 2025-26 from $60.68 billion in 2024-25.
These countries accounted for about 9 per cent of India's total merchandise imports in the last fiscal.
The trade gap was in the favour of India. Some of the European nations are major investors in India, and they include the Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Sweden and Denmark.

articles.title: Europe’s defense billions will only boost the wider economy if policy is designed for it - finchannel
articles.summary: Europe’s defense billions will only boost the wider economy if policy is designed for it  finchannel
articles.full_text:
Europe is preparing to spend up to EUR 800 billion on rearmament. A new Kiel Report by Nathan Lane shows that the money can strengthen Europe’s wider economy, but only if policy is designed for it: spillovers to the civilian economy are not automatic, and procurement, the largest lever of defense industrial policy, is also the least understood.
The report sets out five design lessons for policymakers.
The EU aims to mobilize as much as EUR 800 billion to rebuild its military-industrial capacity. In Germany alone, the 2027 defense budget will reach EUR 140 billion, by far, the largest genuinely discretionary item in the federal budget. The question now is how to design this spending to foster innovation and strengthen industrial capacity across the economy. The Kiel Report “Defense Promotion and Industrial Development” reviews international evidence on R&D tax credits, grants, and public procurement, including defense programs in the US and Europe.
“We cannot assume spillovers from defense are inevitable; they must be engineered by tilting policy toward high-spillover activities,” says Nathan Lane, economist at the London School of Economics and author of the Kiel Report.
Public support crowds private investment in, but returns are concentrated
The evidence is consistent: public innovation support generally triggers additional private investment in research and capital rather than replacing it. Effects on patents, productivity and new firms are positive but vary more. Returns are concentrated among small and medium-sized enterprises, new entrants, and financially constrained firms. Defense R&D, however, is dominated by a small number of large prime contractors.
Whether defense spending benefits the civilian economy is contested. Secrecy, export controls and highly specialized military technology limit transfer to civilian uses. At the same time, mission-oriented wartime research and modern dual-use programs have produced lasting benefits for the wider economy.
“Europe is set to spend billions on defense. This presents a historic opportunity to use defense spending as a tool of industrial policy. But spending alone will not determine the outcome. What matters crucially is how these policies are designed. Nathan Lane reminds us of what research tells us about effective industrial policy: Effective industrial policy should target specific binding constraints rather than apply broad interventions, address institutional and informational barriers alongside financial ones, leverage well-designed public procurement, prioritize activities with high spillover benefits, and be supported by strong administrative capacity,” says Katharina Erhardt, Head of the Industrial Policy Lab at the Kiel Institute.
Procurement matters most, and is understood least
According to Lane, the evidence does not match what is at stake. “The instruments we understand best are not the ones that now matter most, especially for the EU,” he says. “As defense budgets expand, the demand for design evidence will outrun its supply where spending is heaviest, and decisions of enormous scale will rest on the thinnest evidentiary base.”
Procurement can create future demand, stimulate R&D, and build production capacity. Complex rules and uncertain follow-on contracts, however, tend to exclude SMEs and favor incumbents. More open tenders, in which firms propose their own technological solutions, and reliable pathways from development contracts to production orders make a measurable difference.
Five lessons for Europe’s defense industrial policy
The report recommends that policymakers:
Target support to where constraints actually bind, rather than spreading it across all firms.
Address informational and institutional barriers, not only financial ones, for example through innovation organizations such as NATO’s DIANA or the Bundeswehr Innovation Center.
Use procurement deliberately as a tool for industrial development.
Prioritize technologies with civilian applications and high spillover potential.
Invest in the administrative capacity needed to design, steer, and evaluate procurement.
“The rearmament now underway will reshape Europe’s industrial base for a generation, regardless of how it is conducted; whether it also leaves behind a stronger, more innovative economy hinges on the arduous task of designing a truly developmental industrial policy,” says Lane.

Chinese prosecutors are seeking to confiscate more than 61,800 Bitcoin tied to a $5.7 billion fraud scheme, days after a U.K. court ruled Chinese law governs victims’ claims to the coins.
- Chinese prosecutors are seeking to confiscate more than 61,800 BTC and other assets linked to an alleged $5.7 billion fraud that affected more than 102,000 investors.
- Prosecutors say Qian Zhimin’s company sold unlicensed wealth-management products, used investors’ money to repay earlier participants and buy assets, and left victims with nearly 20 billion yuan in losses.
- A British court ruled that Chinese law should govern victims’ claims to the Bitcoin seized in Britain, while a Chinese court has opened a six-month period for interested parties to join the confiscation case.
Chinese prosecutors have moved to seize more than 61,800 Bitcoin linked to a massive fraud case worth over 40 billion yuan, roughly $5.7 billion, according to reporting by Chinese outlet The Paper.
The case centers on Qian Zhimin, the alleged controller of Tianjin Lantian Gree Electronic Technology. Prosecutors say that from 2014 to 2017, the company sold unlicensed wealth-management products across China, promising guaranteed principal and high returns. The scheme raised more than 40.378 billion yuan from more than 102,000 investors, who lost nearly 20 billion yuan.
This money, however, was allegedly used to repay earlier investors, run fake investment projects, buy Bitcoin and acquire property, cars and jewelry, instead of funding real businesses.
Qian then fled China in 2017 and later settled in the UK. British authorities eventually seized his assets, including more than 61,800 bitcoin, plus bitcoin cash, bitcoin gold, bitcoin SV, ripple, dogecoin, cash, jewelry and investment holdings.
On Oct. 13, Tianjin’s Second Intermediate People’s Court said it had accepted prosecutors’ request to confiscate the assets as illegal gains. The court has opened a six-month period for victims and other interested parties to join the case. Victims who do not participate can still seek refunds from recovered assets.
The development comes days after a U.K. High Court ruled that Chinese law, rather than English law, should govern alleged victims’ claims to the more than 61,000 BTC seized in Britain.
The ruling doesn’t mean that victims can never recover their coins. Instead, it calls for assessing whether the victims have a property claim under Chinese law, with further hearings expected. Lawyers for some victims are seeking to appeal.
The case is one of China’s largest alleged crypto-linked frauds—and the Bitcoin stash could be worth far more today than when it was seized.

articles.title: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven - Euronews.com
articles.summary: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Finland, Germany and Lithuania share the euro and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate, but with September inflation at 2.7%, 3.3% and 6.1% respectively, they show how one policy meets different price realities.
Three countries share one currency and one central bank rate, yet their inflation rates differ by more than twofold.
In September, annual inflation was 2.7% in Finland, 3.3% in Germany and 6.1% in Lithuania, according to Eurostat’s harmonised index (HICP), published in October. The euro-area average was 3.8%. All three face the same European Central Bank (ECB) deposit rate of 2.50%.
An energy shock felt unevenly
The common thread is energy. Eurostat data show energy prices across the euro area rose 18.9% in September, adding 1.71 percentage points to inflation, almost half the headline figure. Excluding energy, euro-area inflation was 2.3%.
How that shock plays out depends on a country’s energy mix, tax choices and the strength of its domestic economy.
Lithuania: energy, taxes and wages
Lithuania sits at the top of the range, and food is not the reason. Eurostat figures show food, alcohol and tobacco inflation at 0.5%, while energy prices jumped 33.0% and services inflation reached 6.9%.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) attributes the surge to elevated energy prices amid continued import dependence, strong domestic demand and higher excise duties. Policy added to the pressure. From January, Lithuania raised the VAT on residential heating, hot water and firewood from 9% to 21%. The government’s draft budget estimated that the heating change alone would add 0.5 percentage points to inflation.
Pressure has spread beyond fuel and heating. Eurostat data put Lithuania’s core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, at 3.9%. The Bank of Lithuania expects average wages to rise 9.4% in 2026, and the European Commission links services inflation to strong pay growth and an 11.1% rise in the minimum wage.
Higher wages may leave many workers better off on average. But pensioners, benefit recipients and low-income households with large energy bills are more exposed. There is also a second-round risk. Labour-intensive service businesses can pass higher wages into prices, keeping inflation elevated after the energy shock fades.
Finland: cushioned and sluggish
Eurostat figures show Finland faced a similar energy shock, with energy inflation at 13.1%, yet headline inflation stayed at 2.7%. The European Commission says Finland’s relatively low reliance on fossil fuels softened the blow. Statistics Finland found that cheaper electricity and owner-occupied housing costs restrained its national consumer price index, even as petrol, diesel and heating oil pushed it up.
Domestic price pressure is weak. According to Eurostat, core inflation was 1.4% and services inflation 1.7%. The Bank of Finland forecasts 10.4% unemployment in 2026, while the Commission expects GDP growth of 0.8%. Statistics Finland reports nominal earnings rose 3.5% year on year in the third quarter, or 1.2% in real terms.
That combination helps explain why another rate rise may seem overly restrictive from Helsinki.
Germany: a spike concentrated in fuel
Germany falls in the middle. Eurostat data show energy inflation at 13.4% and core inflation at 2.5%. Germany’s statistics office, Destatis, found motor fuels up 37.1% and heating oil up 74.9% in the national index. Excluding those two items, inflation was 1.8%.
Wage pressure is moderate. Negotiated wages rose 2.9% year on year in August, and the Bundesbank projects the same average for 2026. Eurostat puts services inflation at 2.8%.
Policy also muddies the picture. Existing federal measures lowered electricity, gas and district-heating prices, and a new fuel-tax cut took effect on 1 October, so it is not included in September’s figures. National interventions can shift measured inflation monthly without changing the underlying European shock.
What a single rate means
The ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, arguing that the Middle East conflict was keeping inflation above target and that the full effects of the energy shock had yet to emerge.
Subtracting national headline inflation from the ECB rate gives a rough real-rate proxy: minus 0.2% in Finland, minus 0.8% in Germany and minus 3.6% in Lithuania. This simple calculation based on ECB and Eurostat figures is not a true measure, since households and firms act on expected inflation and face different borrowing costs.
The policy tensions differ by country. Finland’s weak growth and high unemployment argue against tightening. In Germany, the rate is easier to defend given core inflation of 2.5%, but September’s acceleration was driven almost entirely by fuel and heating oil. In Lithuania, the rate looks loose against 6.1% inflation, though higher rates cannot reverse a VAT increase or lower imported fuel prices. They work by weakening demand and curbing second-round effects.
Transmission also varies. ECB research finds that policy works faster and more strongly where variable-rate debt and household leverage are more common, and Lithuania is among the countries relying on variable-rate mortgages with short reset periods.
Yet a recent study covering 2000 to 2025 suggests output and inflation responses to monetary policy are less uneven than often assumed, as some structural differences offset each other.
Sources: Eurostat, ECB, IMF, European Commission, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Finland, Statistics Finland, Destatis, Bundesbank.
